root_cause: Slow query regression on order_items exhausted the Postgres connection pool
root_cause_detail: orders-api v4.9.2 enabled analytics joins by default on the order search path. order_items has not been analyzed in 9 days, so the planner chose a seq scan; orders_search_by_customer now averages 4.2s. Each request holds a connection for 4.2s, so 200 connections are consumed in ~90 seconds and everything else queues for 4-5s. The Redis pool is at 41/100 with no RedisTimeout errors - the recalled payment-api precedent does not apply.
resolution: Added a concurrent index on order_items(customer_id) and disabled the analytics join by default, then ANALYZE order_items. Query p95 back to 190ms, pool at 61/200.
contributing_factors: order_items was not ANALYZEd after the last bulk load, so the planner used a seq scan
A feature flag defaulted analytics joins on, so the risky query entered the default path
Connection pool size (200) was equal to Postgres max_connections, leaving no headroom for admin/migration traffic
Responding to the same alert text as the payment-api incidents encouraged a Redis-shaped response
prevention: Set application pool max well below max_connections (60% rule) and alert on saturation
Add a query budget check in CI that fails when p95 query time regresses more than 3x
Auto-analyze large tables after bulk loads
Run ANALYZE on schedule for order_items
runbook_changes: Add 'is it the database or the cache?' as an explicit first branch in the orders-api latency runbook
Add the pg_stat_statements top-total_time query as step 2
Link the Redis pool incident runbook with an explicit 'not applicable when the cache pool is below 50%' note
lessons: Historical memory is precedent, not proof: the Redis pool exhaustion memory from INC-A1/INC-A2 was recalled and explicitly rejected because redis_connections_active was 41/100 with no RedisTimeout errors.
Restarting pods cannot fix a slow query - it re-establishes 200 connections onto the same query, and pg hit max_connections again in 25 seconds.
A connection pool sized equal to the database's max_connections guarantees that one slow query becomes a total outage.
The highest-information check here was one query: total_time from pg_stat_statements.
first_checks: which dependency is saturated: cache pool or database pool
when was the last ANALYZE on the tables in the failing query
confirmed_by: db_query_p95 below 500ms and pool below 50% of max for 5 minutes
memory_episode: INC-B1 (orders-api, SEV-2): order creation p95 rose to 6.4s with 503s and 'too many clients already' from Postgres. Cause: the v4.9.2 analytics join on the order search path ran a 4.2s seq scan over order_items and consumed all 200 pool connections. Redis was healthy at 41/100, so the earlier Redis pool memories did not apply. Resolved by indexing order_items(customer_id), disabling the analytics join and ANALYZEd the table. Check first next time: which pool is saturated (cache or database) and the pg_stat_statements top total_time query.
memory_service_pattern: orders-api depends on postgres-orders with a 200-connection pool equal to max_connections. Its characteristic failure is a slow-query regression on order_items / order search that saturates the pool. Do not reach for the Redis playbook here: check the database pool first. Restarting pods makes it worse (max_connections in 25s).
